references.text: The immediate context: Jesus uses the fig tree and all trees as a parable. [ref:Luk 21:29|Luke 21:29] introduces the parable that verse 30 continues, where the budding of the trees is a visible sign that summer is near.

The parallel passage in Matthew's version of Jesus' end-times discourse. [ref:Matt 24:32-33|Matthew 24:32-33] recounts the same parable about the fig tree: "When its branches become tender and leaves sprout, you know that summer is near." The wording is very similar to Luke's version.

The parallel passage in Mark's version of the end-times discourse. [ref:Mark 13:28-29|Mark 13:28-29] includes the same parable about the fig tree as a sign, where by seeing the leaves sprout one can understand that summer is near.

The following verse [ref:Luk 21:31|Luke 21:31] gives the interpretive key to the parable: Just as the budding of the trees shows that summer is near, so the signs show that the kingdom of God is near.

James also uses the image of the farmer waiting for the earth's fruit as a picture of patient waiting. [ref:Jak 5:7-9|James 5:7-9] urges patience because the Lord's coming is near – the same theme of recognizing that something great is near.

[ref:Høys 2:11-13|Song of Solomon 2:11-13] describes the signs of spring – the fig tree bearing fruit, the vine blossoming – as natural signs that a new time is breaking in. The image of trees budding as a sign of an approaching season has its background in this kind of nature observation in the Old Testament.

In [ref:Luk 12:54-56|Luke 12:54-56] Jesus rebukes the crowd because they can interpret weather changes, but cannot interpret the time they live in. The same principle underlies 21:30: to observe visible signs and understand (γινώσκετε ἀφʼ ἑαυτῶν) for yourselves what they mean.
